headline: KP governor’s rule stalls electoral reforms, CEC appointment
description: ISLAMABAD - The government seems to be fighting on two fronts – formation of a parliamentary committee on electoral reforms and the appointment of the
author: Javaid-ur-Rahman
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - The government seems to be fighting on two fronts – formation of a parliamentary committee on electoral reforms and the appointment of the chief election commissioner (CEC). The two tasks have become difficult for the ruling coalition after its decision to impose governor rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province as the opposition Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) now wants the government to reverse the move in order to make it two moves successful. The Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Reforms (PCER) will chalk out a plan for electoral reforms revisiting the previous electoral reforms framed in 2017.

The Prime Minister (Leader of the House) and the (Leader of the Opposition) in the National Assembly, under the constitution, jointly consult to recommend three names for the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC). Both the Leader of the House and the Leader of the Opposition have yet to formally deliberate on the names for the appointment of a new Chief Election Commissioner, despite a reminder from the Prime Minister. Interestingly, the process regarding the appointment of new chief election commissioner was formally started with the letter of leader of opposition in the national assembly Mehmood Khan Achakzai. Now, the opposition is reluctant to finalize the pending process. The currently serving Chief Election Commissioner Sikandar Sultan Raja has been in office for over a year after the expiry of their constitutionally mandated five-year terms.

However, a proviso inserted into Article 215(1) through the26th Constitutional Amendment supported him to stay on his seat until the appointment of a new chief election commissioner. Likewise, the appointments of Sindh and Balochistan ECP members are also pending due to delay in the meeting. When contacted, constitutional expert/ former secretary election commission of Pakistan Kanwar Dilshad said that the government is making all out efforts to form a Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Reforms (PCER) but the pending matter of appointing new chief election commissioner is still unresolved. “The new chief election commissioner’s opinion on PCER will be meaningful for next general polls,” he said, mentioning that the opposition should prioritize the matter regarding appointment of new chief election commissioner.

He said the leader of opposition needs to step forward and share names with the government for new CEC as per the constitutional norms. “The proposed names from both sides are deliberated, but process has still not started,” he said, adding that the present chief election commissioner can hold his position until the appointment of a new chief election commissioner. The leader of opposition Mehmood Khan Achakzai, around a month ago, had written a letter to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif seeking immediate appointment of a new chief election commissioner, as well as two members representing Sindh and Balochistan. Achakzai, in the letter, drew the prime minister’s attention to a constitutional duty and stated that the statutory tenure of the CEC and the members representing Sindh and Balochistan had ended on Jan 26, 2025.

The terms of the three officials ended on Jan 26, 2025. Unde Article 215(4) of the Constitution, appointments to these posts were required within 45 days after the positions became vacant by March 12, 2025. Political and constitutional experts viewed that the opposition leader can expedite the matter by proposing the names for new chief election commissioner.

Earlier, former Leader of the Opposition in National Assembly Omar Ayub had also written a letter to the leader of the house /Prime Minister for the appointment of a new chief election commissioner. It may also be noted here that the Prime Minister had also twice offered the opposition to sit with him to resolve pending and controversial matters. On the other hand, Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry has rejected the impression that the government was deliberately delaying the appointment of a new Chief Election Commissioner (CEC), saying the process would be completed in accordance with the Constitution.

“Any attempt to delay the process of appointing the Chief Election Commissioner is not true. The Prime Minister has responded to the letter by the Leader of the Opposition for appointing the CEC,” the minister told The Nation. He said the appointment of the new CEC, along with ECP members from Sindh and Balochistan, would be processed according to constitutional requirements.

Recently, the government and opposition have recently initiated consultations to resolve the long-pending appointments of a new CEC and two ECP members from Sindh and Balochistan. The tenure of CEC Sikandar Sultan Raja expired on January 26, 2025. However, a proviso inserted into Article 215(1) through the 26th Constitutional Amendment allows the incumbent to continue until a successor is appointed. The appointments of ECP members from Sindh and Balochistan are also pending.

description: ISLAMABAD - The Supreme Court of Pakistan Tuesday stated that the dignity of a woman, whether as a wife, sister, daughter, mother or a fellow citizen, is a
author: Shahid Rao
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - The Supreme Court of Pakistan Tuesday stated that the dignity of a woman, whether as a wife, sister, daughter, mother or a fellow citizen, is a fundamental value protected by the Constitution. A two-member bench, headed by Justice Ayesha A Malik, and comprising Justice Shahid Waheed, dismissed an appeal of former employee of the Intelligence Bureau (IB) against the Federal Service Tribunal’s (FST) order. Jawad Abbasi, who used to work as a cook in the IB, had filed an appeal against the verdict of the FST dated January 15. The Tribunal had upheld Abbasi’s compulsory retirement from the service.

He had faced disciplinary proceedings under the Civil Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 2020 over allegations that he had set his wife on fire and was ill-mannered and short-tempered. Abbasi was also accused of conduct that was criminal, unprofessional and prejudicial to good order and service discipline. The departmental proceedings found the charges established, and by an order dated June 14, 2024, he was penalised with compulsory retirement. His departmental appeal in the case had also been rejected, and his appeal pertaining to his service had been dismissed by the FST. However, lower court acquitted him in the criminal case in the matter.

Before the SC, his counsel Aftab Alam Yasir argued that the matter at hand was a private and domestic one between the married couple, had no connection with the petitioner’s official duties, and that Abbasi’s conduct outside his workplace and office hours could not constitute misconduct under the Civil Servants Rules. The counsel pointed out that his client had previously been acquitted by a trial court, further claiming that his wife had attempted suicide. He contended that the rejection of Abbasi’s plea following the departmental inquiry was erroneous. In his judgement on the matter, Justice Waheed observed that the dignity of a woman, whether as a wife, sister, daughter, mother or a fellow citizen, was a fundamental value protected by the Constitution. “Respect for that dignity is not merely a matter of personal morality; it is an obligation that the state is entitled to expect from every person in its service,” the judgement said.

It added that the conduct of a civil servant was not judged exclusively by the manner in which he performed his official duties. His character, integrity and conduct in private life may also become relevant where these factors bore upon his suitability to hold a public office, the discipline of the service or public confidence in the institution he served, Justice Waheed emphasised. A person’s conduct towards those within his own home may, in appropriate circumstances, reveal qualities of character that could not be disregarded merely because the conduct occurred beyond the workplace, the judgement said.

“The walls of a home are not a jurisdictional boundary, and violence does not become private because it is committed behind a closed door,” Justice Waheed stated, adding that “fire does not become a family affair because it was lit indoors”.

“The allegation is not of a quarrel or a harsh word. It is that the petitioner set his wife on fire, an act which, if established, is among the gravest forms of violence one person can inflict upon another,” the judgement said. It further stated: “It is no incident of married life; it is an assault on life and the dignity of a human being.”

The court also observed that the first information report (FIR) in the case was registered under Section 324 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), which carried the penalty for an attempt to murder, and that burn injuries to the woman independently attracted the provisions on hurt in Chapter XVI (offences affecting the human body) of the PPC.

The legislature had classified such conduct as a public wrong against the state, not a private dispute to be settled between spouses, the judgement said, adding that the right to life under Article 9 of the Constitution and the inviolability of the dignity of a person under Article 14 protected a wife within her home as fully as any citizen in a public place.

“The Constitution does not stop at the threshold of a home; it walks in with every woman who lives there,” the judgement said. Moreover, Article 25(3) permitted special provision for the protection of women, and the legislature had acted upon it through, among other enactments, the Punjab Protection of Women against Violence Act, 2016 and the Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act, 2020 for the Islamabad Capital Territory, the court observed.

In addition, Pakistan was a party to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women under which violence against women was recognised as a form of discrimination that the state must act to eliminate, the judgement said.

“The burning of women in their homes, frequently passed off as a kitchen or stove accident or as attempted suicide, is a grave and recurring social evil in this country,” stated Justice Waheed. “The plea of suicide is often the final injury inflicted upon a burnt woman; having been robbed of her safety, she is then robbed of the truth, and her suffering is recast as her own doing,” he said in the judgement, adding that a public institution could not remain unconcerned about such an allegation against one of its own employees and that indifference would be a failure of institutional duty, not a mark of respect for privacy.

“Conduct of this gravity bears directly on the petitioner’s suitability for public service. A civil servant found, on proper inquiry, to have used potentially lethal violence against his own spouse displays a want of self-control and a disregard for human life,” the court declared. It observed that such conduct was “wholly unbecoming” of a government servant and prejudicial to good order and service discipline.

“Where he then seeks to escape responsibility by casting the blame upon the victim, claiming that she set herself alight, he adds deceit to violence. A man who sets his wife on fire and then calls it her suicide has failed twice, first as a husband and then as a witness to the truth; such a man cannot be called a gentleman,” the court ruled. The judgement said public confidence in the civil service rested on the assurance that those who served the state respected the dignity of those around them and a civil servant who denied that respect to his own wife forfeited the trust on which his office depended.

It said, “Public service is a trust, and the conduct of those who hold it is a matter of public concern, at home as much as at work,” the judgement said. “Respect for women is not a private virtue that a civil servant may practice or neglect as he pleases; it is part of the character [of] the state.”

headline: DRAP’s drug pricing mechanism under legal scrutiny as IHC seeks record
description: ISLAMABAD - The Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan’s (DRAP) mechanism for imposing and enforcing maximum retail prices (MRP) on pharmaceutical
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - The Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan’s (DRAP) mechanism for imposing and enforcing maximum retail prices (MRP) on pharmaceutical products has come under judicial scrutiny after a pharmaceutical company challenged the legality of the regulatory approach before the Islamabad High Court. The company through its lawyer Advocate Muhammad Zeeshan Akhtar has questioned the legal basis for extending an existing price-control mechanism to a product which, despite containing the same active ingredient as another regulated formulation, has a different concentration, formulation and intended therapeutic use.

The dispute concerns a product, Pyodine Surgical Scrub Solution 7.5% (60ml), containing Povidone-Iodine, against which DRAP authorities allegedly sought to enforce a maximum retail price by relying upon the pricing framework applicable to Povidone-Iodine 10% solution. Through a constitutional petition filed under Article 199 of the Constitution, M/s Brookes Pharmaceuticals has challenged the issuance of an Explanation Letter dated 16 September 2026, as well as subsequent coercive measures, including seizure of stock and prohibition against disposal of the product. The petitioner has maintained that the distinction between Povidone-Iodine 10% solution and Povidone-Iodine 7.5% surgical scrub is material for regulatory and pricing purposes. It has questioned whether a product can lawfully be subjected to a maximum retail price merely because it contains the same active ingredient as another product included in the National Essential Medicines List (NEML).

The petition further questions whether the relevant price-control provisions under the Drug Pricing Policy, 2018, can be invoked in the circumstances, particularly when the applicability of the pricing framework to the subject product itself is disputed.

The matter has also brought into focus the legal limits of DRAP’s enforcement powers, including the authority to seize pharmaceutical stock and restrict its disposal under Sections 18 and 19 of the Drugs Act, 1976, without adequately establishing the statutory basis for such action. Advocate Zeeshan Akhtar has approached the Islamabad High Court, contending that the impugned actions lack lawful authority and adversely affect its legitimate business activities. The petitioner has also invoked constitutional protections under Articles 4, 10-A and 18 of the Constitution. Taking cognizance of the questions raised, the IHC has observed that the contentions require consideration, particularly regarding whether the subject product falls within the regulatory framework governing fixation and enforcement of maximum retail prices. The Court has specifically identified the distinction between Povidone-Iodine 10% solution and Povidone-Iodine 7.5% surgical scrub, and its legal significance for price regulation, as an issue requiring examination in light of the relevant law and regulatory record. The Court has called upon DRAP and the other respondents to submit comments and a statement along with the relevant record concerning the classification of the subject product, its applicable price, the seizure proceedings and the approval or continuation of the prohibition against disposal.

The Court has also directed that the competent officer appearing on behalf of DRAP explain the statutory justification for the continued seizure and restriction upon disposal of the petitioner’s stock, including the necessity for maintaining such measures pending determination of the alleged violation. While the question of interim relief has been kept for consideration after receipt of the respondents’ position, the Court has directed that the seized stock be maintained under prescribed storage conditions to ensure that its quality and integrity are not compromised during the proceedings.

The Court has called upon DRAP and the other respondents to submit comments and a statement along with the relevant record concerning the classification of the subject product, its applicable price, the seizure proceedings and the approval or continuation of the prohibition against disposal.

The Court has also directed that the competent officer appearing on behalf of DRAP explain the statutory justification for the continued seizure and restriction upon disposal of the petitioner’s stock, including the necessity for maintaining such measures pending determination of the alleged violation. While the question of interim relief has been kept for consideration after receipt of the respondents’ position, the Court has directed that the seized stock be maintained under prescribed storage conditions to ensure that its quality and integrity are not compromised during the proceedings.

headline: FCC rules acquittal no bar to government jobs
description: ISLAMABAD - The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) Tuesday dismissed the Lahore High Court verdict, which denied appointment of the petitioner on account of
author: Shahid Rao
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) Tuesday dismissed the Lahore High Court verdict, which denied appointment of the petitioner on account of his previous involvement in a criminal case. A two-member bench, headed by Chief Justice FCC Amin-ud-Din Khan, and comprising Justice Ali Baqar Najafi heard an appeal of Abdul Latif against the Lahore High Court (LHC).

According to the facts, Abdul Latif, having secured second position in the merit list for the post of Driver Constable, was denied appointment on account of his previous involvement in a criminal case, notwithstanding his acquittal vide judgment dated 11.10.2018 and subsequent issuance of police character certificates reflecting no criminal record.

His representation was rejected by the competent authority on 02.09.2024, whereafter his writ petition and subsequent Intra-Court Appeal were dismissed by the High Court vide judgments dated 10.04.2025 and 22.05.2025, respectively. Hence, the instant petition for leave to appeal was filed. The FCC judgment said that a fundamental distinction must be maintained between the mere registration of an FIR and judicially established culpability. An FIR is merely an accusatory instrument and constitutes neither proof nor presumption of guilt. Once an accused has been acquitted by a competent court, the appointing authority cannot disregard such adjudication or treat the underlying accusation as established misconduct. Although the authority retains discretion to assess a candidate’s antecedents and suitability, such discretion must be exercised bona fide, on objectively verifiable material and strictly in accordance with law.

The judgment said that the competent authorities should accordingly review and harmonize their recruitment policies with the foregoing principles, subject to the applicable statutory framework. Administrative discretion cannot be employed to perpetuate an unproved criminal accusation as an indelible stigma or perpetual impediment to public employment. Such safeguards are indispensable to preserving institutional integrity, public confidence and the rule of law.

It noted that mere involvement in a criminal case, followed by acquittal, cannot, in the absence of independently established adverse material, constitute a perpetual disqualification from public employment. Any contrary approach would substitute administrative suspicion for judicial determination, offending the constitutional principles of legality, fairness and equal protection of law.

The Police Rules, 1934, govern recruitment, appointment and antecedent verification within the Police Department. Rule 12.18 thereof must be construed in harmony with the statutory scheme and constitutional principles of legality, fairness and non-arbitrariness. While antecedent verification serves the legitimate objective of maintaining the integrity and discipline of the police force, such authority cannot be extended to impose disqualifications beyond those contemplated by law.

The FCC said that mere involvement in a criminal case, culminating in acquittal prior to recruitment, cannot, ipso facto, constitute a perpetual disqualification from public employment. Any contrary interpretation would impermissibly enlarge the scope of Rule 12.18 and substitute administrative suspicion for judicial determination, contrary to the maxim expressing facit cessare tacitum. Administrative discretion must, therefore, remain confined to its statutory purpose and be exercised upon legally sustainable grounds.

The judgment in order to emphasize the necessity of uniform, transparent and constitutionally compliant standards governing antecedent verification in public recruitment, asked the competent federal and provincial authorities, particularly law-enforcement agencies, to ensure adherence to the following guiding principles:

Mere registration of an FIR shall not ipso facto constitute a disqualification from public employment. Judicial acquittal shall receive due recognition, subject to an objective assessment of the candidate’s antecedents and suitability. Adverse character verification shall be founded upon authentic. independently verifiable material rather than conjecture or suspicion

Upon acquittal, the criminal case shall not be reflected adversely in the Police Character Certificate; where proceedings remain pending, only their pendency shall be disclosed, without any presumption of guilt. No candidate shall ordinarily be excluded without a meaningful opportunity of hearing and a reasoned determination. Recruitment decisions shall conform to the prescribed statutory criteria, merit, proportionality and constitutional guarantees of fairness and equality.

headline: Kumail Shah calls on Punjab Governor Saleem Haider Khan
description: SUKKUR - Chairman District Council Sukkur, Syed Kumail Hyder Shah, held an important meeting with Governor Punjab Sardar Saleem Haider Khan at the Governor
author: Our Staff Reporter
article_text:
SUKKUR - Chairman District Council Sukkur, Syed Kumail Hyder Shah, held an important meeting with Governor Punjab Sardar Saleem Haider Khan at the Governor House, Lahore.

According to district council’s release issued here on Tuesday, both leaders exchanged views on matters of mutual interest and the overall political situation of the country.

The meeting also featured detailed discussion on making the local government system more active, effective and empowered, besides deliberations on the role of local bodies and resolution of public issues.

Syed Kumail Hyder Shah said that there is a need to make local governments more effective, active and empowered. He said that through a strong local government system, public issues can be resolved at their doorstep. He said that the Pakistan Peoples Party believes in public service and has always struggled for the rights of the people. He added that Sindh is moving towards progress under the leadership of the Peoples Party. Governor Punjab Sardar Saleem Haider Khan said that politics is about serving the people and practically resolving their difficulties and issues.

headline: Three more fake teacher appointments exposed in Mirpurkhas, total reaches nine
description: MIRPURKHAS - Another recruitment scam has surfaced in the Education Department of Mirpurkhas, with the appointments of three more teachers declared fake,
author: Our Staff Reporter
article_text:
MIRPURKHAS - Another recruitment scam has surfaced in the Education Department of Mirpurkhas, with the appointments of three more teachers declared fake, raising the total number of such cases to nine. The scandal has also exposed alleged illegal appointments and the disbursement of salaries through the Treasury Office.

In this regard on Tuesday, taking notice of a report submitted by Director of School Education (Primary), Mirpurkhas, Muhammad Iqbal Kumbhar, the Secretary Education has directed the Director of School Education Hyderabad to conduct an inquiry.

According to official reports, the appointments of Muhammad Imran (HST), Bhaghchand (JST) and Muhammad Usman (JST) have been found to be fake. The revelations prompted Director of School Education Muhammad Iqbal Kumbhar to formally inform the Secretary Education, following which the Director of School Education (Primary), Hyderabad, initiated a departmental inquiry into the matter.

Earlier, the appointments of six teachers, including Mir Fahad Ali, Anil Kumar, Shah Rukh Khan, Abida Parveen, Zahid Ali and Arshad Ali, had also been declared fake, bringing the total number of identified cases to nine.

The repeated exposure of fraudulent appointments in Sindh’s Education Department has raised concerns over recruitment procedures, verification of official records and the payment of salaries to allegedly ineligible employees through the Treasury Office.

The ongoing inquiry is expected to examine the circumstances surrounding the appointments and the alleged financial irregularities.

headline: Commissioner assures Hindu community of full support for Diwali celebrations
description: HYDERABAD - Commissioner Shaheed Benazirabad Division, Ghulam Qadir Khan Talpur, on Tuesday assured the Hindu community of all possible facilities and
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
HYDERABAD - Commissioner Shaheed Benazirabad Division, Ghulam Qadir Khan Talpur, on Tuesday assured the Hindu community of all possible facilities and security arrangements for the upcoming festival of Diwali.

He gave this assurance during a meeting with Rajesh Kumar Hardasani, Member of the National Paigham-e-Aman Committee Pakistan and representative of the Hindu Panchayat, at his office.

During the meeting, matters relating to arrangements for Diwali celebrations, maintenance of law and order, and provision of necessary facilities to the Hindu community were discussed. Rajesh Kumar Hardasani briefed the commissioner on the administrative requirements for the upcoming festivities. The commissioner said that deputy commissioners and senior superintendents of police (SSPs) across the division had been directed to make appropriate arrangements to ensure peaceful celebrations and facilitate the Hindu community. He emphasised that it was the administration’s responsibility to provide all religious communities with an environment in which they could celebrate their religious festivals freely and with dignity, respect and happiness.

He said that promoting religious harmony, interfaith tolerance and brotherhood was essential for building a peaceful and prosperous society. He added that citizens belonging to all religious communities were an integral part of society and that effective coordination among relevant departments was necessary to ensure their rights, security and access to essential facilities.

The commissioner stressed the need to promote mutual respect, unity, peace and love on the occasion of Diwali and other religious festivals to further strengthen interfaith harmony.

Rajesh Kumar Hardasani thanked the commissioner for assuring full cooperation in making Diwali arrangements and highlighted the importance of collective efforts to promote peace and religious harmony.

Additional Commissioner-II Shaheed Benazirabad Syed Ammar Hussain was also present at the meeting.

headline: KU forms committee over law college results
description: KARACHI - A three-member committee comprising representatives of the Supreme Court, Sindh High Court, and the Federal Higher Education Commission has been
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
KARACHI - A three-member committee comprising representatives of the Supreme Court, Sindh High Court, and the Federal Higher Education Commission has been constituted to conduct impartial and transparent investigations into complaints regarding the second-year results and mark sheets of the University of Karachi’s affiliated law colleges.

The committee will present its fact-based report to the University administration after thoroughly examining, considering, and discussing the matter with all stakeholders. This process will include meetings with affected students, copy checkers, and individuals responsible for reviewing answer scripts following scrutiny requests. The members will also visit the Examination Department and hold discussions with the Controller of Examinations and other relevant officials. According to details, certain students had pointed out alleged discrepancies and errors in the announced examination results. They maintained that they had successfully passed the examinations, yet were declared unsuccessful in the issued mark sheets. In this regard, affected students submitted formal scrutiny requests, claiming that they were entitled to be declared successful in the B.A./LL.B examinations.

It was clarified that, under prevailing rules, the scrutiny process allows only for re-totaling or re-counting of marks, whereas re-evaluation of answer scripts does not fall within the scope of scrutiny. In view of the legal and administrative dimensions of the matter, the University of Karachi resolved to ensure an independent and transparent inquiry. Accordingly, a three-member committee has been formed, comprising Justice (R) Zia Pervez, Justice (R) Nadeem Akhtar, and Dr Nazir Hussain of the Federal Higher Education Commission. The committee has been entrusted with fact-finding responsibilities and will review all relevant records and evidence before submitting its report to the KU administration, so that the matter may be resolved on a priority basis in a fair and transparent manner.

The Committee, which was constituted last week, will have its first meeting at the Vice Chancellor Secretariat, on Wednesday, November 04, at 12:00 noon. It was also decided that a comprehensive academic calendar for the affiliated law colleges will be prepared, encompassing all teaching, academic, and examination activities throughout the year. This calendar will be presented for approval in the next meeting of the KU Academic Council which will take place in the current month.

The University of Karachi reiterates its unwavering commitment to transparency, fairness, and accountability at every stage of its academic and administrative processes. The institution firmly believes in upholding merit, discouraging any form of wrongdoing, and ensuring that corrective measures are taken wherever required.

By establishing independent committees and strengthening grievance mechanisms, KU continues to demonstrate its resolve to safeguard the trust of its students and stakeholders, and to maintain the integrity of its examination and evaluation systems.

headline: Cabinet committee constituted to resolve issues related to Katchi Abadis: Sharjeel
description: KARACHI - Sindh Senior Minister for Information, Transport and Mass Transit Sharjeel Inam Memon has said that the Sindh Cabinet has approved reducing the
author: Our Staff Reporter
article_text:
KARACHI - Sindh Senior Minister for Information, Transport and Mass Transit Sharjeel Inam Memon has said that the Sindh Cabinet has approved reducing the release price of government wheat from Rs5,000 to Rs4,500 per 40 kilograms, resulting in a reduction of Rs17 per kilogram in flour prices.

He said that the Cabinet had also approved the registration of Lady Dufferin Hospital Trust under the Sindh Trust Act 2020. In addition, ex-post facto approval was granted to a programme, supported by the Asian Development Bank (ADB), for preparing an investment programme worth $1 billion for urban development in five divisional headquarters of Sindh. Under this programme, projects related to water supply, drainage, sanitation and solid waste management will be prepared.

The Cabinet also approved the Draft Rules 2026 for the registration and monitoring of charitable organisations under the Sindh Charities Registration and Regulation Act 2019. Addressing a press conference after the Sindh Cabinet meeting in Karachi, Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon said that the Sindh Cabinet had approved additional funds amounting to Rs502.409 million for five development schemes in Jamshoro district.

These schemes also include funds for the water supply scheme in Sehwan city and the installation of RO plants. Similarly, the Cabinet approved a development scheme worth Rs2 billion, 99 crore, 34 lakh and 26 thousand for the improvement of the water supply and drainage system in Nawabshah Town, Shaheed Benazirabad district. He said that a Cabinet Committee had been constituted to resolve matters related to katchi abadis (informal settlements). headline: Govt plans gradual shift to electric vehicles for official fleets
description: ISLAMABAD - The government plans to gradually replace federal and provincial government vehicles with electric and other low-emission alternatives
author: APP
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - The government plans to gradually replace federal and provincial government vehicles with electric and other low-emission alternatives under a proposed Green Government Fleet Project to reduce fossil-fuel consumption, cut transport related emissions and limit exposure to fluctuating fuel prices. The initiative aims to establish a scalable model for decarbonising public-sector transport while demonstrating government leadership in promoting clean mobility. Under the proposed framework, a comprehensive inventory of government vehicle fleets will be prepared, documenting vehicle types, ages, mileage, fuel consumption and emissions to establish a baseline for phased replacement. The assessment will identify vehicles suitable for conversion to electric or other low-emission alternatives and prioritise government departments for the transition. The project also envisages procuring and deploying electric vehicles and other clean transport options, alongside installing charging infrastructure at government offices, depots and other priority facilities.

Green procurement standards and lifecycle-cost assessments will guide vehicle replacement decisions to ensure the selection of appropriate technologies and cost-effective alternatives.

A digital fleet-monitoring system will also be introduced to track vehicle utilisation, energy and fuel consumption, maintenance needs and reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

The proposed initiative further includes specialised training for fleet managers, drivers and maintenance personnel to strengthen operational capacity and ensure the effective management of clean vehicle fleets.

Under the institutional framework, the federal government, through relevant ministries and divisions, will provide policy direction, identify priority departments and vehicles, and coordinate implementation arrangements.

Government agencies will oversee vehicle deployment, operational data and fleet management, while procurement and fleet management entities will facilitate the development of green procurement specifications and replacement plans.

Power-sector institutions and electricity distribution companies will support charging connections and assess electricity requirements, while vehicle manufacturers and charging-infrastructure suppliers will provide equipment, technical assistance and maintenance services.

Climate-related institutions will ensure alignment with national climate mitigation objectives and help monitor the project’s environmental benefits.

The implementation framework envisages infrastructure planning, phased procurement and deployment of clean vehicles, commissioning of charging facilities, and continuous operational monitoring and staff training.

The project’s performance will be assessed through indicators including reductions in fuel consumption, operating costs and greenhouse gas emissions.

headline: ANF seizes over 302 kg of drugs in 9 operations, arrests 10 suspects
description: Rawalpindi - The Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF)on Tuesday conducted nine operations in various cities across the country and seized 302.49 kg of
author: APP
article_text:
Rawalpindi - The Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF)on Tuesday conducted nine operations in various cities across the country and seized 302.49 kg of narcotics, arresting 10 suspects, including a woman.

In an intelligence-based operation near Kuchlak Bypass, the ANF recovered 210 kg of morphine from a secret hideout.

In Peshawar, 26.4 kg of drugs were seized from a secret compartment of a vehicle near a BRT stop on University Road, leading to the arrest of a suspect.

In Burewala, Vehari district, 10.8 kg of hashish and 7.2 kg of opium were recovered from a suspected vehicle near the post office, and two individuals were apprehended. The ANF also seized 9.6 kg of hashish from a vehicle near Pindorian, Islamabad and arrested two suspects.

In Gujranwala, 6 kg of hashish was recovered from a man and a woman travelling on a motorcycle on GT Road near Chanda Qila, while 5 kg of hashish was seized from a motorcyclist near Sehrish Nagar, Hyderabad.

During an international drug interdiction operation, ANF intercepted 16 ladies’ bags containing ice at a private cargo office at Allama Iqbal International Airport, Lahore. The bags had a gross weight of 11.290 kg and were destined for Australia. In inter-provincial operations, 9.6 kg of hashish was seized from a suspect near Ravi Toll Plaza, Lahore, while another 6.6 kg was recovered from a vehicle near the Motorway Toll Plaza, Islamabad, leading to the arrest of an accused.

Cases have been registered against the arrested suspects under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and further investigation is underway.

headline: Over 756,000 children administered polio drops on first day of campaign
description: Rawalpindi - Over 756,000 children were administered polio drops across the district on the first day of the ongoing anti-polio campaign, while
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
Rawalpindi - Over 756,000 children were administered polio drops across the district on the first day of the ongoing anti-polio campaign, while authorities have intensified efforts to cover all remaining missed children.

This was shared during a meeting chaired by Deputy Commissioner Rawalpindi, Captain (retd) Nadeem Nasir, on the second day of the drive to review the performance of the opening day. The meeting was attended by Additional Deputy Commissioner Social Services Fazail Mudassar, the chief executive officer Health, and other relevant officers.

During the briefing, officials informed the deputy commissioner that 58,104 children were initially identified as missed on the first day due to various reasons. Out of these, 32,708 children were successfully covered on the same day through prompt field intervention, while measures are actively underway to reach the remaining 25,396 children. The forum was further briefed that specialized sweep-up activities were completed in low-coverage and missed pockets across the district to ensure maxium coverage. Directing officers to ensure that every missed child receives the polio vaccine, DC Nadeem Nasir emphasized the effective execution of the micro-plan, strictly monitored field activity, and the continuous presence of vaccination teams on the ground. He stressed that no child should be left unvaccinated during the campaign.

author: Ali Raza

BAHAWALNGAR - Bahawalnagar Deputy Commissioner on Tuesday visited Haider Stadium Bahawalnagar and directed the authorities to start repair and restoration work immediately. According to the details, Deputy Commissioner Syed Muhammad Abbas Shah visited Haider Stadium Bahawalnagar in detail and reviewed the stadium building, sports field and facilities available to the players.

On this occasion, District Sports Officer, Deputy Director Development and other concerned officers were also present. While inspecting the current condition of the stadium, the Deputy Commissioner directed the concerned officers to start all the necessary repair and restoration work immediately and complete these within the stipulated time. He said that the facilities available in the stadium should be further improved so that the players can be provided with a suitable environment for sports activities. The Deputy Commissioner further directed that quality should be ensured in the improvement and renovation works of the stadium and all matters should be completed on a priority basis so that citizens and young athletes can get better sports facilities.

headline: Past in Perspective
description: The Faraday law of electromagnetic induction, discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831, showed how changing a magnetic field could result in the generation of an
author: The Nation
article_text: The Faraday law of electromagnetic induction, discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831, showed how changing a magnetic field could result in the generation of an electric current. This fundamental principle laid the groundwork for the development of electrical generators, transformers, and motors, revolutionising technology and power distribution. Today, Faraday’s law is integral to the functioning of electrical systems worldwide, from power plants to household appliances. It underpins the generation of electricity from renewable energy sources like wind and hydroelectric power, driving sustainable energy production and shaping the transition to a greener future.

headline: Harming US’s Global Standing
description: The United States and Israel, seemingly oblivious to Iran’s formidable resilience, have waged a war whose consequences are difficult to comprehend. Trump
author: The Nation
article_text:
The United States and Israel, seemingly oblivious to Iran’s formidable resilience, have waged a war whose consequences are difficult to comprehend. Trump believed that eliminating Iran’s leadership would bring about the country’s collapse within a week. However, the resilience and determination of the Iranian people have proved him wrong. The war is costing the United States billions of dollars, damaging its economy and eroding public trust in Trump. During his election campaign, he pledged to prevent wars around the world, yet he has now started a conflict with no clear end in sight.

Trump’s blind trust in Israel has drawn public condemnation, with critics labelling him a warmonger seeking to overthrow governments that oppose his policies. Iran had been pursuing negotiations with the United States to ease hostilities. However, under the pretext that Iran was developing nuclear weapons, the US launched attacks, fundamentally changing the situation in the Middle East. Iran retaliated by targeting US bases across the region, putting American personnel at risk and damaging its defensive capabilities. The conflict has also drawn other Gulf countries into an increasingly volatile situation.

Peace might have been possible had the United States not attacked Iran and its nuclear facilities. In the early days of the war, a US strike on an elementary school reportedly killed 146 girls, an incident that raises serious questions about violations of international law. Israel has drawn the United States into a predicament that its administration may not have anticipated.

Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz has further intensified the crisis, disrupting shipping and driving up international oil prices, with consequences for the US economy as well. There is no clear indication of when the war might end. If it continues, the entire world could face dangerous repercussions.

Iran has spent decades preparing for a confrontation with the United States and Israel, building substantial stockpiles of ammunition and missiles and developing drones that have challenged the perceived superiority of American weapons. The US reportedly uses interceptors costing millions of dollars to destroy a single, relatively inexpensive Iranian drone. Iran has also encouraged allied militias in Iraq and Lebanon to target US bases and Israeli military installations, putting further pressure on both countries.

The American public has grown increasingly frustrated with Trump over what many regard as an unnecessary war. Some critics have accused him of diverting public attention from the Epstein files, in which his name has been mentioned. Iran is unlikely to accept US influence and appears determined to continue resisting it, regardless of the extent of American and Israeli military action.

headline: The Missing Shield
description: The death of five-year-old Ayat Noor in Haripur should disturb Pakistan far beyond the horror of the crime. She disappeared near her home, remained missing for
author: The Nation
article_text:
The death of five-year-old Ayat Noor in Haripur should disturb Pakistan far beyond the horror of the crime. She disappeared near her home, remained missing for days, and was eventually found dead. The post-mortem examination indicated sexual assault and fatal blood loss. Although CCTV footage, geofencing and other investigative measures helped police identify suspects, the tragedy raises a crucial question: why does a missing child not immediately trigger the fastest possible response from the state?

Ayat’s death is not an isolated incident. During the first six months of 2026, Sahil documented 3,172 reported cases of gender-based violence, including 644 murders, 462 abductions, 280 rapes and 132 honour killings. More than half occurred in victims’ homes, highlighting that danger does not always come from strangers or unfamiliar places.

These figures expose an uncomfortable reality: safety cannot be ensured simply by asking families to remain vigilant or women to restrict their movements. Protecting children and women is ultimately a public responsibility.

Pakistan has taken important legislative steps. The Anti-Rape (Investigation and Trial) Act 2021 provides for specialised procedures and Anti-Rape Crisis Cells, bringing medical, forensic, legal and psychological assistance together. However, these provisions must translate into effective action.

Every missing-child report should trigger an immediate investigation, rapid risk assessment and effective use of technology. Police officers, medico-legal staff and prosecutors need specialised training, while forensic facilities must be equipped to preserve and examine evidence without delay. Institutional accountability is equally essential.

The alleged sexual assault of a woman inside a Lahore police station exposed the consequences of institutions meant to provide protection becoming sources of vulnerability. Similarly, attributing serious offences to mental instability without proper assessment only risks obscuring responsibility.

Public debate must also move beyond demands for harsher punishments. Deterrence depends not only on severe sentences but on ensuring that offenders are identified, prosecuted and held accountable.

Pakistan’s problem is not simply a shortage of laws, but a lack of certainty: that missing children will be searched for immediately, evidence preserved, survivors treated with dignity and investigations completed without procedural delays.

Ayat Noor’s life cannot be restored. But her death must prompt a stronger national response in which protecting children and women is recognised not as sympathy after tragedy, but as a fundamental responsibility of the state.

RANA MUHAMMAD FAZEEL DASTGIR,

Lahore.

unfamiliar places.

These figures expose an uncomfortable reality: safety cannot be ensured simply by asking families to remain vigilant or women to restrict their movements. Protecting children and women is ultimately a public responsibility.

Every missing-child report should trigger an immediate investigation, rapid risk assessment and effective use of technology. Police officers, medico-legal staff and prosecutors need specialised training, while forensic facilities must be equipped to preserve and examine evidence without delay. Institutional accountability is equally essential.

The alleged sexual assault of a woman inside a Lahore police station exposed the consequences of institutions meant to provide protection becoming sources of vulnerability. Similarly, attributing serious offences to mental instability without proper assessment only risks obscuring responsibility.

Public debate must also move beyond demands for harsher punishments. Deterrence depends not only on severe sentences but on ensuring that offenders are identified, prosecuted and held accountable.

Pakistan’s problem is not simply a shortage of laws, but a lack of certainty: that missing children will be searched for immediately, evidence preserved, survivors treated with dignity and investigations completed without procedural delays.

Ayat Noor’s life cannot be restored. But her death must prompt a stronger national response in which protecting children and women is recognised not as sympathy after tragedy, but as a fundamental responsibility of the state.

author: Dr Kamal Monnoo
article_text:
There was considerable excitement when the revolutionary economist and leader Javier Milei took over the reins of Argentina. Much was expected of him by a people who had endured extreme hardships for a long time. In contrast, the current ruling lot in Pakistan may not have come to power on a similar wave of popularity, but given the track record of the PML-N and the economic results under direct military rule, much was also expected of this combination, albeit on the economic front.

Truth be told, economic results in both Argentina and Pakistan are falling short of expectations. Let us compare the salient economic features under the two administrations, given the many similarities in what they inherited, despite being geographically far apart.

In Milei’s case, his administration has delivered a dramatic, highly polarised macroeconomic stabilisation plan that has crushed inflation and balanced the budget, but at the cost of a deep economic contraction, business closures and significant public hardship. Pakistan seems little different.

Approaching his third year in office, Milei’s ‘chainsaw austerity’ has transformed Argentina’s economic landscape into a stark two-speed economy. Pakistan presents a similar picture, where the divide and disparity have increased significantly, creating two distinctly different worlds: one for the masses, being pushed deeper into poverty, and the other for a select segment that can drive the meaningless headline numbers our economic managers often quote to justify their performance.

1) Defusing Hyperinflation: Milei took office in late 2023, inheriting an annual inflation rate of 211 per cent. Through aggressive fiscal adjustments, monthly inflation has been reduced to below 2 per cent, bringing annual inflation down to around 31–33 per cent by late 2026, arguably one of the most rapid turnarounds in recent monetary history.

By contrast, Pakistan fortunately did not face such extreme inflation or hyperinflation. Still, the government can be credited with bringing inflation close to single digits, at least officially. Unofficially, inflation in real terms still hovers around 15–16 per cent, something indirectly confirmed by the SBP’s recent decision to raise interest rates by 50 basis points.

2) Fiscal and Trade Surpluses: For the first time in 14 years, Argentina has consistently posted budget surpluses. The administration eliminated multiple federal ministries, laid off over 50,000 public employees, halted public works and lifted strict currency controls.

No such luck in Pakistan, where the external account remains under pressure, imports, especially non-essential ones, remain stubbornly high, and the size of government and its perks have actually swelled from an already unhealthy level. Meanwhile, the seemingly impressive foreign exchange reserves are, in essence, largely borrowings.

3) Booming Resource Export Sectors: Driven by deregulation, Argentina’s sovereign credit ratings have been upgraded. Record-breaking extraction from the Vaca Muerta shale formation turned the country’s energy deficit into a multibillion-dollar trade surplus, alongside surges in lithium mining and agriculture.

Ironically, this is where Pakistan has faltered badly, and policy failures are most glaring and damaging. Pakistani exports continue to slip, deindustrialisation, particularly among SMEs, is proceeding rapidly, and a misplaced focus on overseas workers’ remittances is driving administrative policy complacency at the expense of productivity and employment-generating domestic investment.

This, in turn, is fuelling public discontent through unemployment and rising poverty. One only has to read the latest World Bank report to ascertain how far south we are heading!

a) A Poverty W-Curve: Poverty in Argentina peaked at over 53 per cent in early 2024 following the initial peso devaluations, then steadily declined to 28.2 per cent by late 2025 as price growth stabilised. However, official INDEC data released in late September 2026 showed a severe setback: poverty rebounded to 32.3 per cent in the first half of 2026, as household incomes failed to keep pace with a 20 per cent spike in the cost of basic goods. Extreme poverty, or indigence, also rose to 7.5 per cent.

This is starkly similar to what has transpired in Pakistan, where poverty has reached almost 50 per cent. Pakistan, by some accounts, is now said to have more people living below the poverty line than even Afghanistan or India.

b) Industrial and Consumer Contraction: While private-sector wages in Argentina have seen isolated growth, public-sector wages have plummeted by 15 per cent in real terms. A plunge in domestic purchasing power has caused a collapse in consumer spending and retail sales. Reports indicate that over 30,000 businesses, heavily concentrated in retail, manufacturing and commerce, have closed due to soaring utility costs and weak domestic demand.

In Pakistan, the industrial contraction has already been outlined, while the contraction in consumer demand is also becoming starkly visible, especially in items of mass consumption.

Foolishly high taxation and coercive, often foolhardy, collection drives have not only sucked efficient capital out of the markets, diverting it into inefficient hands and uses, but have also drained investor confidence.

Multinational companies are exiting or are eager to leave at the first available opportunity, since the cumulative tax burden, by the time money reaches the pockets of final shareholders, can touch 60 per cent or more. Who in their right mind would want to operate in such an environment, particularly amid an incompetent and corrupt oversight mechanism?

c) Labour Rebalancing: Argentina’s official unemployment rate edged upwards to nearly 8 per cent in 2026. To cope, hundreds of thousands of workers have migrated from the formal sector into informal and self-employed roles.

Pakistan’s situation is even worse, given its large population, particularly its young, employable people aged 35 or under. Nearly four million people enter the labour market every year in an economy where, dangerously, jobs are becoming scarcer with each passing day. Some analysts estimate unemployment at nearly 25 per cent, including disguised unemployment of around 8–10 per cent.

Politically, Milei capitalised on his initial momentum during the October 2025 midterm elections, when his party, La Libertad Avanza, won nearly 41 per cent of the vote, dramatically expanding its presence in Congress and allowing him to push through sweeping tax and labour modernisation laws.

However, entering late 2026, the protracted domestic recession, alongside administrative scandals, has strained public patience, pulling his approval ratings below 40 per cent and setting the stage for a highly contested political environment ahead of future electoral cycles.

Here, too, in Pakistan, the government’s public acceptance is rapidly deteriorating. Frustration among the masses is high, and the sooner we re-strategise economic policies around public needs and growth aspirations, the better it will be for all stakeholders.

On a separate note, however, personal popularity drives aside, one cannot help but be impressed by the recent initiatives undertaken by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif. Perhaps the centre could also take a leaf or two out of her economic strategy manual!

Dr Kamal Monnoo The writer is an entrepreneur and economic analyst. Email: kamal.monnoo@gmail.com

2) Fiscal and Trade Surpluses: For the first time in 14 years, Argentina has consistently posted budget surpluses. The administration eliminated multiple federal ministries, laid off over 50,000 public employees, halted public works and lifted strict currency controls.

No such luck in Pakistan, where the external account remains under pressure, imports, especially non-essential ones, remain stubbornly high, and the size of government and its perks have actually swelled from an already unhealthy level. Meanwhile, the seemingly impressive foreign exchange reserves are, in essence, largely borrowings.

3) Booming Resource Export Sectors: Driven by deregulation, Argentina’s sovereign credit ratings have been upgraded. Record-breaking extraction from the Vaca Muerta shale formation turned the country’s energy deficit into a multibillion-dollar trade surplus, alongside surges in lithium mining and agriculture.

Ironically, this is where Pakistan has faltered badly, and policy failures are most glaring and damaging. Pakistani exports continue to slip, deindustrialisation, particularly among SMEs, is proceeding rapidly, and a misplaced focus on overseas workers’ remittances is driving administrative policy complacency at the expense of productivity and employment-generating domestic investment.

This, in turn, is fuelling public discontent through unemployment and rising poverty. One only has to read the latest World Bank report to ascertain how far south we are heading!

a) A Poverty W-Curve: Poverty in Argentina peaked at over 53 per cent in early 2024 following the initial peso devaluations, then steadily declined to 28.2 per cent by late 2025 as price growth stabilised. However, official INDEC data released in late September 2026 showed a severe setback: poverty rebounded to 32.3 per cent in the first half of 2026, as household incomes failed to keep pace with a 20 per cent spike in the cost of basic goods. Extreme poverty, or indigence, also rose to 7.5 per cent.

This is starkly similar to what has transpired in Pakistan, where poverty has reached almost 50 per cent. Pakistan, by some accounts, is now said to have more people living below the poverty line than even Afghanistan or India.

b) Industrial and Consumer Contraction: While private-sector wages in Argentina have seen isolated growth, public-sector wages have plummeted by 15 per cent in real terms. A plunge in domestic purchasing power has caused a collapse in consumer spending and retail sales. Reports indicate that over 30,000 businesses, heavily concentrated in retail, manufacturing and commerce, have closed due to soaring utility costs and weak domestic demand.

In Pakistan, the industrial contraction has already been outlined, while the contraction in consumer demand is also becoming starkly visible, especially in items of mass consumption.

Foolishly high taxation and coercive, often foolhardy, collection drives have not only sucked efficient capital out of the markets, diverting it into inefficient hands and uses, but have also drained investor confidence.

Multinational companies are exiting or are eager to leave at the first available opportunity, since the cumulative tax burden, by the time money reaches the pockets of final shareholders, can touch 60 per cent or more. Who in their right mind would want to operate in such an environment, particularly amid an incompetent and corrupt

oversight mechanism?

c) Labour Rebalancing: Argentina’s official unemployment rate edged upwards to nearly 8 per cent in 2026. To cope, hundreds of thousands of workers have migrated from the formal sector into informal and self-employed roles.

Pakistan’s situation is even worse, given its large population, particularly its young, employable people aged 35 or under. Nearly four million people enter the labour market every year in an economy where, dangerously, jobs are becoming scarcer with each passing day. Some analysts estimate unemployment at nearly 25 per cent, including disguised unemployment of around 8–10 per cent.

Politically, Milei capitalised on his initial momentum during the October 2025 midterm elections, when his party, La Libertad Avanza, won nearly 41 per cent of the vote, dramatically expanding its presence in Congress and allowing him to push through sweeping tax and labour modernisation laws.

However, entering late 2026, the protracted domestic recession, alongside administrative scandals, has strained public patience, pulling his approval ratings below 40 per cent and setting the stage for a highly contested political environment ahead of future electoral cycles.

Here, too, in Pakistan, the government’s public acceptance is rapidly deteriorating. Frustration among the masses is high, and the sooner we re-strategise economic policies around public needs and growth aspirations, the better it will be for all stakeholders.

On a separate note, however, personal popularity drives aside, one cannot help but be impressed by the recent initiatives undertaken by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif. Perhaps the centre could also take a leaf or two out of her economic strategy manual!

Dr Kamal Monnoo

The writer is an entrepreneur and economic analyst. Email: kamal.monnoo@gmail.com

headline: Healing Amid Hostility
description: A hospital is responsible not only for diagnosing and treating patients but also for providing psychological comfort. Healthcare professionals can fulfil
author: Tehreem Fatima
article_text:
A hospital is responsible not only for diagnosing and treating patients but also for providing psychological comfort. Healthcare professionals can fulfil these responsibilities effectively only when they themselves feel safe and supported. However, recent incidents have shown how this essential environment is increasingly being disrupted by disputes between healthcare workers and patients’ attendants.

Two incidents that attracted widespread attention on social media illustrate this troubling situation. On 7 September 2026, at the Rawalpindi Institute of Cardiology, a nursing officer was reportedly physically assaulted by patients’ attendants following a dispute over hospital rules and overcrowding. On 18 October, at Gulab Devi Hospital in Lahore, a female doctor and female attendants became involved in a physical confrontation over the treatment of a critically ill patient.

Although the circumstances differed, both incidents raised serious concerns about healthcare workers’ safety and the quality of patient care. Why are places dedicated to saving lives increasingly becoming scenes of confrontation?

One major cause is the shortage of healthcare resources. As a nursing student, I have witnessed critically ill patients and their families facing distressing situations while waiting for essential facilities, including ventilator support. Overcrowding, insufficient beds, staff shortages, inadequate equipment and limited critical-care facilities place enormous pressure on public hospitals.

When patients experience delays or cannot access the treatment they need, their families understandably become distressed. Unfortunately, this frustration is often directed towards doctors and nurses, without considering the limitations under which they work. Healthcare professionals also experience emotional stress when inadequate resources prevent them from providing the standard of care they have been trained to deliver. During my clinical training, I have often felt guilt and helplessness in such situations, even when the circumstances were beyond my control.

Another major factor is ineffective communication between healthcare professionals, patients and their attendants. Inadequate explanations, unclear instructions and a lack of regular updates can create confusion, anxiety and mistrust.

Healthcare workers sometimes use technical terminology without explaining it in language that families can understand. Consequently, attendants may misunderstand the seriousness of a patient’s condition, the purpose of treatment or the reasons for delays. They may interpret insufficient information as negligence, even when medical staff are performing their duties responsibly.

Communication becomes particularly challenging during emergencies, when families experience intense emotional distress. Denial and anger, as described in Kübler-Ross’s stages of grief, can influence how people process difficult news. Without compassionate communication, misunderstandings can escalate into arguments and even physical confrontations.

Healthcare professionals must therefore communicate with empathy and clarity, while attendants should express concerns respectfully and allow medical staff to perform their duties.

Limited public understanding of hospital procedures further contributes to these conflicts. Many attendants are unfamiliar with emergency triage, the prioritisation of critically ill patients and restrictions in intensive care units.

Families may expect immediate attention without realising that emergency departments prioritise patients according to the urgency of their conditions. When such procedures are poorly explained, delays can be mistaken for discrimination or negligence.

Public awareness campaigns are essential to educate citizens about emergency services, hospital regulations, patients’ rights and their responsibilities towards healthcare workers. However, none of these circumstances can justify violence. Disagreements must be resolved peacefully, and allegations of misconduct investigated fairly.

Addressing these challenges requires coordinated efforts. The government must strengthen public healthcare through greater investment, adequate staffing, improved emergency facilities and the availability of essential medicines and equipment.

Schools, universities and media platforms should promote health literacy, patience and mutual respect. Healthcare institutions must also emphasise therapeutic communication, ensuring that professionals approach distressed patients and families with compassion.

Equally important is hospital security. Controlled access, functioning CCTV systems, trained security personnel and clear protocols for responding to threats can help protect staff. Violence must be investigated promptly, while patients and families should have accessible channels for reporting genuine concerns.

Ultimately, responsibility extends beyond the government. Every individual must help create an environment of understanding and respect for those working tirelessly to protect public health.

Hospitals should be places where patients find comfort, families find reassurance and healthcare professionals can work without fear. Restoring this environment requires stronger institutions, better communication and mutual respect.

As the saying goes, ‘No one should have to choose between caring for their community and protecting their own safety.’

Tehreem Fatima The writer is a third-year Generic BSN student at College of Nursing, King Edward Medical University Lahore.

One major cause is the shortage of healthcare resources. As a nursing student, I have witnessed critically ill patients and their families facing distressing situations while waiting for essential facilities, including ventilator support. Overcrowding, insufficient beds, staff shortages, inadequate equipment and limited critical-care facilities place enormous

pressure on public hospitals.

When patients experience delays or cannot access the treatment they need, their families understandably become distressed. Unfortunately, this frustration is often directed towards doctors and nurses, without considering the limitations under which they work. Healthcare professionals also experience emotional stress when inadequate resources prevent them from providing the standard of care they have been trained to deliver. During my clinical training, I have often felt guilt and helplessness in such

situations, even when the circumstances were beyond my control.

Another major factor is ineffective communication between healthcare professionals, patients and their attendants. Inadequate explanations, unclear instructions and a lack of regular updates can create confusion, anxiety and mistrust.

Healthcare workers sometimes use technical terminology without explaining it in language that families can understand. Consequently, attendants may misunderstand the seriousness of a patient’s condition, the purpose of treatment or the reasons for delays. They may interpret insufficient information as negligence, even when medical staff are performing their duties responsibly.

Communication becomes particularly challenging during emergencies, when families experience intense emotional distress. Denial and anger, as described in Kübler-Ross’s stages of grief, can influence how people process difficult news. Without compassionate communication, misunderstandings can escalate into arguments and even physical confrontations.

Healthcare professionals must therefore communicate with empathy and clarity, while attendants should express concerns respectfully and

allow medical staff to perform their duties.

Limited public understanding of hospital procedures further contributes to these conflicts. Many attendants are unfamiliar with emergency triage, the prioritisation of critically ill patients and restrictions in intensive care units.

Families may expect immediate attention without realising that emergency departments prioritise patients according to the urgency of their conditions. When such procedures are poorly explained, delays can be mistaken for discrimination or negligence.

Public awareness campaigns are essential to educate citizens about emergency services, hospital regulations, patients’ rights and their responsibilities towards healthcare workers. However, none of these circumstances can justify violence. Disagreements must be resolved peacefully, and allegations of misconduct investigated fairly.

Addressing these challenges requires coordinated efforts. The government must strengthen public healthcare through greater investment, adequate staffing, improved emergency facilities and the availability of essential medicines and equipment.

Schools, universities and media platforms should promote health literacy, patience and mutual respect. Healthcare institutions must also emphasise therapeutic communication, ensuring that professionals approach distressed patients and families with compassion.

Equally important is hospital security. Controlled access, functioning CCTV systems, trained security personnel and clear protocols for responding to threats can help protect staff. Violence must be investigated promptly, while patients and families should have accessible channels for reporting genuine concerns.
Ultimately, responsibility extends beyond the government. Every individual must help create an environment of understanding and respect for those working tirelessly to protect public health.

Hospitals should be places where patients find comfort, families find reassurance and healthcare professionals can work without fear. Restoring this environment requires stronger institutions, better communication and mutual respect.
As the saying goes, ‘No one should have to choose between caring for their community and protecting their own safety.’

Tehreem Fatima

The writer is a third-year Generic BSN student at College of Nursing, King Edward Medical University Lahore.

headline: Buried Alive in Silence
description: In the first six months of this year, 3,172 cases of violence against women and girls were officially recorded in Pakistan: 644 murders, 514 cases of torture,
author: Fe’reeha Idrees
article_text:
In the first six months of this year, 3,172 cases of violence against women and girls were officially recorded in Pakistan: 644 murders, 514 cases of torture, 462 abductions, 280 rapes and 132 ‘honour’ killings. These figures come from the six-month Cruel Numbers report by Sahil, a Pakistani organisation working to protect children from abuse and exploitation.

This is only the tip of the iceberg. According to the Peace and Justice Network’s National Gender-Based Violence Report 2021–2025, a staggering 237,216 crimes against women and girls were reported to the police over five years. And that counts only those who dared to reach a police station.

The provincial breakdown should shake any conscience. Punjab accounted for 195,787 cases, or 82.5 per cent of the national total. Sindh followed with 25,107, of which 77 per cent, or 19,289, involved kidnappings and abductions. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, home to 16.5 per cent of Pakistan’s population, reported only 10,210 cases, but cultural taboos prevent many incidents from being reported. Of 2,334 domestic violence cases reported in KP, 1,197 ended in murder. By the time the complaint reached the police, the woman was already dead. Balochistan reported 3,108 cases, but geographic isolation, tribal pressures and institutional failure obscure the true scale.

In 2024 alone, according to police data cited by the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, 4,175 rapes and 733 gang rapes were registered nationwide. Last week in Lahore, five women were raped in different localities within seven days, including a divorced mother of seven who drives a rickshaw to feed her children.

Behind every number is a name. And in recent years, the names have become impossible to ignore.

In Sindh, it was Fatima Fariro, the ten-year-old maid tortured to death in a feudal lord’s haveli in Khairpur. In Karachi, 18-month-old Aizal died after an alleged sexual assault by a teenage relative. In KP, five-year-old Ayat Noor was abducted in Haripur and later found dead in an unused well. In Balochistan, Dr Mahnoor Nasir, a 29-year-old surgery trainee, had acid thrown on her face in her duty room by a hospital lift operator who had harassed her for months.

In Islamabad, Sarah Inam, a 37-year-old economist, was murdered by her husband, while 17-year-old TikToker Sana Yousaf was killed after refusing a marriage proposal. Rizwana, a 12-year-old housemaid from Sargodha, was brutally tortured in the Islamabad home of a civil judge’s family. Most recently, in Rawalpindi, 45-year-old digital media executive Hina Javed was found dead in her bathroom, her hands tied, mouth gagged and a wire around her neck. Her brother told police she had repeatedly reported abuse.

And yet, conviction remains a fantasy. According to a briefing to the Senate Functional Committee on Human Rights in May, rape conviction rates for 2025 stood at 4 per cent in Punjab, 6 per cent in KP, 12 per cent in Balochistan and 22 per cent in Sindh. The national conviction rate for honour killings still hovers at 0.5 per cent.

The status of women in Pakistan needs serious re-examination. While the world has moved forward, with women standing alongside men, we have lagged far behind. Intoxicated by the opium of cultural superiority, we have denied women both the modern rights progressive societies guarantee and the divine rights Islam ensured fourteen hundred years ago.

A deeper study of Islam shows that women have far more rights than we are taught: the rights to inheritance, divorce, honour, education and property. These are not favours granted by men. These are divine rights.

Consider Hina Javed, who delayed marriage to care for her mother with dementia and later delayed divorce to avoid the stigma of being called a divorced woman. Her story mirrors thousands of others in which women choose silence over so-called stigma.

We have normalised naming and shaming women. It has become acceptable. On Pakistan’s streets, men move like idle spectators, believing they have the right to ogle at women. We have given ogling social recognition. Cheap jokes about women are treated as a prerogative of masculinity. What kind of country is this, where a woman cannot run freely in a park? Why does a grown, educated, taxpaying woman need a car, a driver and a chaperone simply to travel from one place to another? These are symptoms of a deeper ailment.

Recently, Maryam Nawaz Sharif tweeted about the fate of a woman expected to suffer in silence. Her words resonated because every Pakistani woman knows that script. Who determines what deserves silence? Why must a woman justify walking out of a relationship? When Allah Himself has given her the choice to enter marriage through nikah and exit through khula, who are we to take that choice away?

Marriage, children and working on relationships matter. But nowhere does it say a woman must compromise until she becomes a slave, or remain silent until death. Yet we live by that cruel proverb that a woman’s funeral should leave her husband’s home, that her janaza should go out only after marriage. How can a society calling itself Islamic allow such an un-Islamic saying to govern its homes?

Pakistan will not progress by keeping women silent. Sahil’s report notes that 60 per cent of gender crimes happen inside the victim’s home, the place supposed to be safest. A nation that teaches its daughters to suffer quietly teaches its sons that silence is consent. It is time our pulpits spoke about Surah An-Nisa. It is time we taught boys that ogling is not masculinity. And it is time we told women that Allah gave them a voice long before society tried to take it away.

Fe’reeha Idrees The writer is a journalist and anchor. She tweets @Fereeha.
